name: Keratin straightening
lead: Keratin straightening, also called a Brazilian treatment, is a salon smoothing procedure in which a keratin-containing product is applied to the hair and sealed in with a flat iron. People get it for smoother, frizz-free, shinier hair that looks sleeker and is quicker to style, which is why it appears in grooming and hair-care discussions. Wikipedia describes it as reducing frizz and adding shine, lasting roughly two to six months, and taking about two to four hours [1].

Unlike chemical relaxers, the effect is described as gradually washing out rather than permanently restructuring the hair, with the hair slowly returning to its original texture [1]. The treatment is listed as suitable for most hair types, including damaged or previously treated hair [1]. Related ingredients are covered in the hydrolyzed keratin entry.

The category has attracted health discussion. Wikipedia notes that keratin treatments emit gases, that skin and eye protection is needed, and that they are not recommended during pregnancy; some straightening products are described as containing formaldehyde-releasing agents [1]. A small registered study of a keratin hair therapy exists, with unknown status [2].

chain: Frizz reduced, cuticle smoothed, shine added
Sleeker, more manageable hair for months
angle.text: The treatment gives smoother, straighter-looking hair for about two to six months, reducing frizz and daily styling time. Results fade gradually as the hair returns to its natural texture.

paras: A layer of keratin, a protein found naturally in hair, is applied and the hair is then flat-ironed with heat; the treatment straightens hair, reduces frizz and adds shine [1]. Aftercare commonly involves avoiding washing, ponytails and clips for about three days [1].

Wikipedia states that fumes are emitted during use, with protective gear required and use not recommended in pregnancy [1]. Its formaldehyde discussion concerns chemical relaxers and straightening products that may contain formaldehyde-releasing agents; it cites a National Institutes of Health study linking such products to breast, uterine and ovarian cancers [1], and links to guidance from the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration on formaldehyde in hair-smoothing products [1]. Heat applied during straightening can damage hair, which Wikipedia says cannot be reversed except by cutting off the damaged hair [1].

A registered study, NCT04489576 (Evaluation of Safety and Efficacy of Keratin Hair Therapy), planned 30 participants with hair damage, began in November 2020, and has unknown status with no posted results [2].

card.summary: Salon keratin-and-heat smoothing that lasts months; some products release formaldehyde, and trial data are scant.
card.note: Fumes and formaldehyde-releasing ingredients are a reported concern; not recommended in pregnancy.

quick.overview:
A keratin straightening treatment coats the hair with a keratin product and seals it with a flat iron, to cut frizz and add shine for a few months.

Published trial evidence is sparse: one small registered study with unknown status.
quick.mechanism: Heat sets the applied coating onto the hair shaft, smoothing the surface; it is described as less structurally permanent than relaxers.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes emitted gases, formaldehyde-releasing agents in some products, protective gear requirements, and advice against use in pregnancy. Heat can also damage hair.
